questions.q: Why does a baseline need to be captured before a change, not just after, per this lesson?
options: SQL Server physically deletes performance data after any schema change
Baselines captured after a change are automatically more accurate
Without a recorded "normal" state to compare against, there's no reliable way to know whether a change actually helped, hurt, or did nothing
It's only required for Azure SQL Database, not on-prem instances
questions.explain: Comparing an after-measurement to a guess or a feeling isn't evidence — you need a real prior snapshot for the comparison to mean anything.

questions.q: What makes Query Store a strong baseline source, per this lesson?
options: It only stores data for queries that fail
It replaces the need for any server-level metrics entirely
It automatically persists historical per-query execution statistics (duration, CPU time, logical reads, execution count) over time, without extra setup once enabled
It is the only way to see the current execution plan for a running query
questions.explain: Once turned on for a database, Query Store keeps historical runtime stats bucketed into intervals automatically, which is exactly what a baseline needs.

questions.q: What's the key limitation of sys.dm_exec_query_stats as a baseline source, per this lesson?
options: It requires Query Store to be enabled first
Its statistics are cumulative since each plan was compiled, and the data empties on plan eviction or a server restart, so you must snapshot and diff over time
It cannot be queried with T-SQL, only through SSMS reports
It only shows statistics for stored procedures, never ad hoc queries
questions.explain: Because the numbers are cumulative and volatile (cleared on eviction/restart), a single read at one point in time isn't a baseline — you need two snapshots to diff.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend also capturing PerfMon/server-wide counters, not just query-level data?
options: Query Store cannot be used on any server that also runs PerfMon
Server-wide counters are required to enable Query Store
PerfMon counters are more accurate than any DMV
A query-level baseline alone can miss the real cause — a query may not have changed at all if the server itself is under more memory or I/O pressure than before
questions.explain: Metrics like Page Life Expectancy or Batch Requests/sec capture system-wide pressure that a single query's stats won't reveal on their own.

questions.q: Why does the lesson warn against capturing a baseline during a single quiet 2 a.m. window?
options: Query Store only records data between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. by default
SQL Server disables all DMVs outside business hours
It won't represent real peak and average load, so comparisons against a busier period will be misleading rather than a fair before/after
Nighttime measurements are always inaccurate due to backup jobs
questions.explain: A baseline should span a representative business cycle (a full day or week, depending on workload pattern) so it reflects the conditions you actually care about tuning for.
